title: Experimental generation of asymmetric keys from the parity structure of a two-photon six-qubit entangled state
authors: Sanchari Chakraborti, Soumya Asokan, Sunita Khoth, Sujai Matta, C. M. Chandrashekar
abstract: We propose and experimentally demonstrate an asymmetric key-generation scheme in which public and private keys are derived from a six-qubit photonic entangled state. A six-qubit entangled state is generated from two photons, each carrying one polarization and two path qubits. The state is prepared in an equal superposition of eight of the sixty-four six-qubit basis states, in which each photon's three qubits form a codeword of the classical [3,2,2] even-parity code, and are distributed between the two parties, Alice and Bob. This ensures, each triple is a uniformly random codeword and the two codewords are locked together through the correlation. The parity constraint is a local stabilizer, so each party verifies it on its own data every round, and eliminates the bit flip errors arising from imperfections, detector dark counts and multiple occupancy before it enters the raw key. A single publicly announced bit, chosen at random from either of the path qubits, allows each party to reconstruct the other's full triple while leaking no information to third party. We realize the desired six-qubit state using a Sagnac-based type-II SPDC source, reporting a Bell-CHSH parameter S = 2.798 +/- 0.008, by implementing gate operation on polarization and path degree's of freedom. This approach provides a physics-based alternative to public-key cryptosystems built on computational hardness assumptions. A t-bit string generated from multiple rounds for encryption will be intrinsically random. Without the private key, one needs at least O(2^t) runs on an t-qubit quantum system to find the matching bit to decrypt.
summary: The authors experimentally demonstrate a quantum key distribution protocol using a six-qubit entangled state generated from two photons. They encode the state using an even-parity code, allowing both parties to perform local error checks round-by-round. This method provides a quantum-secure alternative to classical cryptography by leveraging fundamental quantum correlations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for quantum-secure, physics-based asymmetric key generation, providing an alternative to cryptosystems relying on computational hardness assumptions.
main_result: They experimentally demonstrated a key generation scheme using a six-qubit photonic entangled state, achieving a high Bell-CHSH parameter ($S = 2.798 \pm 0.008$) and demonstrating built-in error detection.
method: The protocol utilizes a six-qubit state derived from two photons, encoding the qubits into a classical [3,2,2] even-parity code, and uses local parity checks for error filtering.
model_or_system: The system is a photonic platform using two photons, each carrying polarization and path qubits. The state is generated via a Sagnac-based type-II SPDC source, and the key relies on the correlations within the parity-constrained six-qubit state.
key_observables: Bell-CHSH parameter ($S = 2.798 \pm 0.008$), Fidelity ($F = 0.987$), Raw key rate ($\approx 131$ kbit/s), and Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER $\approx 4.61\%$).
important_parameters: The key rate is doubled by generating two private bits per round. The security relies on the difficulty of guessing the random $t$-bit string, requiring $O(2^t)$ runs.
main_assumptions: The security is based on the monogamy of shared entanglement, and the local self-check mechanism assumes that errors are independent noise sources.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum circuit for state preparation, the experimental setup using SPDC, and measurements confirming polarization entanglement and the Bell-CHSH parameter.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical construction of the six-qubit state using the [3,2,2] code, outlines the key generation protocol involving public announcement and private reconstruction, and concludes with experimental measurements verifying entanglement and key rate.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, hardware-implementable demonstration of quantum key distribution that moves beyond simple entanglement swapping by incorporating error-correcting code structures into the key exchange protocol itself.
